unit.can_do_en: talk about Midsummer and Christmas and give dates.

brief.situation_en: Aino and Maria in early June.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: What are you doing at Midsummer?

judge.reason: Only register difference: sä vs sinä.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: En tiiä vielä. Millon se on?
lines.text_kirja: En tiedä vielä. Milloin se on?
lines.gloss_en: I don't know yet. When is it?

judge.reason: tiiä/tiedä and millon/milloin are register variants; negation and meaning are the same.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Kesäkuun lopus. Se on aina lauantaina.
lines.text_kirja: Kesäkuun lopussa. Se on aina lauantaina.
lines.gloss_en: At the end of June. It's always on a Saturday.

judge.reason: lopus/lopussa is a register variant; the rest is identical.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: What do Finns do at Midsummer?

judge.reason: Spoken 'tekee' with a plural subject is normal colloquial usage for 'tekevät'.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Ne menee mökille, saunoo ja polttaa kokkoja.
lines.text_kirja: He menevät mökille, saunovat ja polttavat kokkoja.
lines.gloss_en: They go to the cottage, have a sauna and light bonfires.

judge.reason: Ne/he and the dropped plural verb endings are register differences; the actions are the same.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Tuu meidän mökille! Siel on tilaa.
lines.text_kirja: Tule meidän mökillemme! Siellä on tilaa.
lines.gloss_en: Come to our cottage! There's room.

judge.reason: Tuu/tule, siel/siellä and meidän mökille/mökillemme are register variants; the same invitation and place.
Oikeesti/oikeasti, kiitti/kiitos and mielellään/mielelläni are register variants; the meaning is the same.

forms.why_en: The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
Tehdä changes to tee- and takes -t for 'you': teet.
Adds -na to say when: juhannus becomes juhannuksena.
Ei with -n for 'I': en, I do not.
After en the verb drops its ending: tietää becomes tiedä. Speech says tiiä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech often drops an i: millon. Books write milloin.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
Adds -n so it goes with lopussa: kesäkuun lopussa, 'at the end of June'.
Adds -ssa for 'in': loppu becomes lopussa, with one p. Speech drops the end: lopus.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Days take -na for 'on': lauantai becomes lauantaina.
Adds -t for more than one: suomalainen becomes suomalaiset.
Books write tekevät. Speech uses the he or she form: tekee.
Speech uses ne for people too. Books write he.
Books write menevät. Speech uses the he or she form: menee.
Adds -lle for 'to': mökki becomes mökille, with one k.
Books write saunovat. Speech uses the he or she form: saunoo.
And: joins the coffee and the bun in the order.
Books write polttavat. Speech uses the he or she form: polttaa.
Kokko becomes kokkoja for bonfires in general, an amount you don't count.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Kuulostaa (to sound) wants -lta: kiva becomes kivalta, 'sounds nice'.
After ei (not), the verb loses its ending: tulee becomes tule. Speech says tuu.
Me takes -dän for 'our': meidän. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: allative singular, with the possessive ending for our
forms.why_en: Books add -lle for 'to' and -mme for 'our': mökillemme. Speech drops -mme: meidän mökille.
Siellä means there. Speech drops the last vowel: siel.
tila, room. 'Some room' ends in -a: tilaa.
Adds -sti to oikea (real) to say how: oikeasti. Speech turns ea into ee: oikeesti.
Thank you, said by the customer; in casual speech it becomes kiitti.

forms.form_name_en: adessive singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Mielelläni means 'gladly' or 'I'd love to'. Speech often says mielellään.
